analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices and offer seniors a cheaper government-run prescription drug plan.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Cardin with no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote and died when that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug law barred the government from negotiating drug prices and set up the Part D benefit so seniors could only buy coverage from private insurers. This bill would repeal that ban, let Medicare itself offer a nationwide drug plan at a $35 monthly premium alongside private options, and pay employers back in full for keeping retiree drug coverage. It was sent to two House committees, then to their health subcommittees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, who would gain a government-run drug plan at a set $35-a-month premium as an alternative to private plans, and benefit from Medicare being allowed to negotiate drug prices with manufacturers. Large employers who cover retirees would gain full federal reimbursement for that coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provision in the 2003 Medicare law that prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering with negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies and prescription drug plan sponsors, restoring the government's authority over drug price structures. [S2] [S3]

Requires the Secretary of HHS to qualify and serve as a prescription drug plan sponsor, offering a nationwide drug plan with basic coverage at a $35 premium for 2006, adjusted annually thereafter — in addition to, not instead of, private plans. [S2] [S3]
Guarantees every Medicare Part D eligible person a choice of at least three plans, including the government-run plan, and requires that area plans come from more than one sponsor. [S2] [S3]
Provides full reimbursement to employers for the cost of qualified retiree drug coverage, and lets retiree plan costs count toward seniors' catastrophic limits. [S2] [S3]
Repeals the Comparative Cost Adjustment program and the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund created by the 2003 law. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would face a government empowered to negotiate prices and set formulary reimbursement structures, and private drug plan insurers would have to compete with a cheaper public plan. Taxpayers would bear the cost of full employer retiree reimbursement and of running the new government plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, private drug insurers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals cost containment provisions added by the 2003 Medicare law, and provides full federal reimbursement of employer retiree drug coverage — both of which would add to federal Medicare spending. [S2]
The $35 government-plan premium is set by statute, so if the plan's actual costs run higher, taxpayers would cover the difference rather than enrollees. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: seniors would likely get lower drug costs through price negotiation and a low-premium public plan, while pharmaceutical makers and private drug plans would lose revenue and taxpayers would pick up new federal costs, including full reimbursement of employer retiree coverage. The bill's repeal of cost-containment provisions and its statutorily set premium mean its long-term federal price tag was a real weakness that an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, sat there with no hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill in the House on May 19, 2005. [S1] [S3]
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction. [S5]
In late May and early June 2005, it was referred to the health subcommittees of both committees. [S5]
No further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private prescription drug plan insurers kept the 2003 law intact, including the ban on Medicare price negotiation and their exclusive role in selling seniors drug coverage. Seniors continued to buy coverage from private plans with no government-run alternative.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plan insurers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and sat in committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 2003 law's prohibition on the government interfering in drug price negotiations and setting formulary reimbursement structures, exposing manufacturers to Medicare-driven price pressure. Drug companies' interest in keeping the ban ran directly against seniors' interest in lower prices. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Private Medicare prescription drug plan (PDP) insurers
industries.note: The bill requires HHS to offer its own nationwide drug plan at a $35 premium as an alternative to private plans, forcing insurers to compete with a cheaper public option. The 2003 law had made private plans the only channel for the new drug benefit. [S2] [S3]
The bill repeals the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund and the Comparative Cost Adjustment program, both of which were federal supports created for regional plans under the 2003 law. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Large employers with retiree drug coverage
industries.note: The bill provides full federal reimbursement for qualified retiree drug coverage and lets those costs count toward seniors' catastrophic limits, lifting a cost from employers while helping retirees keep coverage. [S2] [S3]
